rules.title: Password spraying / brute force (many failed logons)
rules.description: A burst of failed logons. Many accounts from one source suggests spraying; one account many times suggests brute force.
rules.recommendation: Identify the source IP/host, block it, and confirm no success (4624) followed. Enforce lockout and MFA.

rules.title: Successful logon after repeated failures (likely cracked)
rules.description: An account that failed to log on many times then succeeded from the same source — the hallmark of a guessed or sprayed password.
rules.recommendation: Reset the account password, review what the session did, and check the source host.

rules.title: Security event log cleared
rules.description: The Security log was cleared. Attackers do this to destroy evidence; it is almost never part of normal operations.
rules.recommendation: Find who cleared it and when, and recover logs from your SIEM or forwarded copies.

rules.title: System/application event log cleared
rules.description: An event log was cleared.
rules.recommendation: Confirm whether this was a sanctioned maintenance action.

rules.title: New service installed
rules.description: A new Windows service was installed whose program looks like a script interpreter or sits in a user-writable path — common for persistence and lateral movement (PsExec-style).
rules.recommendation: Inspect the service's binary path and signature; remove it if not legitimate.

rules.title: Scheduled task created
rules.description: A scheduled task was created that runs a script host or a user-folder program.
rules.recommendation: Review the task action and trigger; remove it if unexpected.

rules.title: Suspicious process creation (command-line rules)
rules.description: Process-creation events are run through the full living-off-the-land rule set, so historical 4688 logs are analyzed the same way as live processes.
rules.recommendation: See the matched command-line rule for specifics.

rules.title: Suspicious PowerShell script block
rules.description: Recorded PowerShell script blocks are scanned with the command-line rules, catching encoded commands, download cradles, AMSI bypasses and reflective loading.
rules.recommendation: See the matched rule; recover the full script block for analysis.

rules.title: PowerShell logging was reduced or disabled
rules.description: A script tried to turn off PowerShell history or script-block logging — covering tracks.
rules.recommendation: Treat subsequent PowerShell activity as under-logged; pull any history that remains.

rules.title: New user account created
rules.description: A new account was created. Normal in managed environments; suspicious on a workstation or outside a change window.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the account is expected and who created it.

rules.title: Member added to a privileged local group
rules.description: An account was added to local Administrators or Remote Desktop Users.
rules.recommendation: Verify authorization; remove and investigate if not.

rules.title: Member added to a privileged domain group
rules.description: An account was added to a highly privileged domain group — a major escalation if unexpected.
rules.recommendation: Confirm with your change process immediately; this is a common post-compromise action.

rules.title: Microsoft Defender protection disabled or configuration changed
rules.description: Microsoft Defender reported being disabled, modified or that it detected malware. Protection changes near other suspicious activity are a red flag.
rules.recommendation: Check what changed, re-enable protection, and review detections.

rules.title: Interactive/RDP logon from an external address
rules.description: An interactive or remote-desktop logon came from a public IP address. Direct RDP from the internet is a common intrusion vector.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the source is expected; restrict RDP exposure and require MFA/VPN.

rules.title: Microsoft Defender detected malware
rules.description: Microsoft Defender reported a malware detection (1116) or an action taken on one (1117). The file was seen on this host; the action may or may not have succeeded.
rules.recommendation: Check the action result (1117 / Protection history), find how the file arrived (parent process, browser download, email) and whether it ran.

rules.title: Command-line tradecraft in Sysmon process creation
rules.description: Runs the command-line rule pack over Sysmon Event 1 (process creation).
rules.recommendation: See the matched rule.

rules.title: Remote thread created in LSASS (Sysmon 8)
rules.description: A process created a thread inside LSASS — a code-injection technique used to steal credentials.
rules.recommendation: Identify the source process, preserve it, and treat credentials on this host as exposed.

rules.title: Suspicious handle opened to LSASS (Sysmon 10)
rules.description: A non-system process opened LSASS with memory-read access rights typical of credential-dumping tools.
rules.recommendation: Identify the source process and whether a dump file was written.

rules.title: Run key set (Sysmon 13)
rules.description: A Run/RunOnce autostart value was written. Many installers do this; review the program it points at.
rules.recommendation: Check the value data and the writing process.

rules.title: Account locked out
rules.description: An account was locked out after repeated failed logons — context for password guessing.
rules.recommendation: Correlate with 4625 failures and their source.

rules.title: Directory replication requested by {SubjectUserName} (DCSync)
rules.description: A user account (not a domain controller) used directory replication rights. This is how DCSync tools such as Mimikatz pull password hashes for every account, including krbtgt.
rules.recommendation: Confirm whether the account is a legitimate replication tool (for example Azure AD Connect). If not, treat all domain credentials as compromised.

rules.title: Directory Services Restore Mode password changed
rules.description: The DSRM administrator password of a domain controller was set. Attackers set it to keep a local backdoor account on the DC.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the change was planned; check DsrmAdminLogonBehavior in the registry.

rules.title: SID history added to {TargetUserName}
rules.description: A SID was added to an accounts SID history. Outside a domain migration this grants hidden privileges (for example Domain Admins).
rules.recommendation: Remove the SID history entry unless a migration is under way; review who made the change.

rules.title: Kernel debugging or test signing enabled at boot
rules.description: The boot configuration allows kernel debugging, test-signed drivers or disabled integrity checks. This lets unsigned drivers and rootkits load.
rules.recommendation: Check bcdedit settings and restore secure defaults.

rules.title: Service runs a command that writes to a named pipe (GetSystem-style)
rules.description: A service was installed whose command echoes into a named pipe. Meterpreter getsystem and similar tools use this to impersonate SYSTEM.
rules.recommendation: Identify the process that owns the pipe and the session that created the service.

rules.title: Service {ServiceName} runs a bare command without a full path
rules.description: Real services point at a full program path. A service that just runs cmd, PowerShell or similar is a common remote-execution trick.
rules.recommendation: Find the remote session that created it (4624 type 3 at the same time) and remove the service.

rules.title: Remote execution pipe {RelativeTargetName} opened from {IpAddress}
rules.description: A remote host opened the service-control or a PsExec-style pipe over SMB. This is how PsExec, Impacket and similar tools start programs on this machine.
rules.recommendation: Confirm the source and account are an authorized admin; look for a 7045 service install at the same time.

rules.title: Program copied to admin share: {RelativeTargetName} from {IpAddress}
rules.description: A remote host wrote an executable into ADMIN$ or C$. Remote-execution tools copy their service binary this way before starting it.
rules.recommendation: Collect the file and find out which tool or person copied it.

rules.title: Authentication-coercion pipe {RelativeTargetName} opened from {IpAddress}
rules.description: A remote host opened a pipe used by PrinterBug, PetitPotam or DPAPI backup-key theft. These pipes also have normal uses, so treat this as context.
rules.recommendation: Check the source host; correlate with machine-account authentications to unexpected hosts.

rules.title: RDP logon for {TargetUserName} from the local machine (tunnelled RDP)
rules.description: A Remote Desktop logon arrived from 127.0.0.1. This happens when RDP is tunnelled through SSH, plink or a port forward to bypass network controls.
rules.recommendation: Find the tunnelling process (plink, ssh, netsh portproxy) and its outside peer.

rules.title: Kerberos network logon for {TargetUserName} from the local machine (possible KrbRelayUp)
rules.description: The built-in Administrator logged on over the network from this machine using Kerberos. KrbRelayUp and similar local privilege escalations produce exactly this.
rules.recommendation: Look for a new machine account or RBCD change and a service created right after.

rules.title: Logon with alternate credentials for {TargetUserName} (pass-the-hash pattern)
rules.description: A type 9 (NewCredentials) logon. runas /netonly does this legitimately; Mimikatz sekurlsa::pth and token-duplication tools do too.
rules.recommendation: Check which process requested it and whether the user normally uses runas /netonly.

rules.title: LSASS opened by {ProcessName}
rules.description: A process requested memory-read access to LSASS. Credential dumping tools do this to read password hashes and tickets.
rules.recommendation: Identify the process and whether a dump file was written.

rules.title: SeDebugPrivilege enabled by {ProcessName}
rules.description: A program running from a user-writable folder turned on the debug privilege, which lets it open any process including LSASS.
rules.recommendation: Identify the program; debug privilege from such a path is typical of credential-theft tools.

rules.title: LSASS dumped through silent process exit monitoring
rules.description: Windows Error Reportings silent-exit monitor was used against LSASS. Tools abuse this to write an LSASS memory dump without opening the process directly.
rules.recommendation: Find the dump in the LocalDumps folder, delete it, and treat the credentials on this host as exposed.

rules.title: NTDS database opened from an unusual location
rules.description: The Active Directory database was opened from a snapshot or a copied folder. ntdsutil IFM and shadow-copy theft of ntds.dit produce this.
rules.recommendation: Find who ran ntdsutil or vssadmin and where the copy went.

rules.title: SQL Server xp_cmdshell enabled or used
rules.description: xp_cmdshell lets SQL queries run operating-system commands. Attackers enable it after getting into a database.
rules.recommendation: Disable xp_cmdshell and review who connected to SQL Server and what ran.

rules.title: Process image tampering: {Image}
rules.description: Sysmon saw a process whose memory image no longer matches the file on disk: process hollowing, herpaderping or doppelganging.
rules.recommendation: Capture the process memory and identify the parent that created it.

rules.title: WMI event subscription created or changed: {Name|Consumer}
rules.description: A permanent WMI event subscription was created. It runs a command or script whenever its trigger fires and survives reboots.
rules.recommendation: List subscriptions (root\subscription) and remove unknown ones.

rules.title: Unsigned or invalid driver loaded: {ImageLoaded}
rules.description: A kernel driver without a valid signature loaded. Rootkits and BYOVD tools need this to disable security products.
rules.recommendation: Identify the driver file and the process that installed it.

rules.title: Remote thread created in {TargetImage} by {SourceImage}
rules.description: One process started a thread inside another. Injectors and C2 implants (Meterpreter migrate, Cobalt Strike) do this to hide in a trusted process.
rules.recommendation: Check the source process and dump the targets memory.

rules.title: {SourceImage} opened {TargetImage} from unbacked memory
rules.description: A process handle was opened by code that does not belong to any loaded module (UNKNOWN in the call stack). That is the signature of injected shellcode.
rules.recommendation: Capture the source process memory.

rules.title: Credential-dump file written: {TargetFilename}
rules.description: A file with the name of a credential dump or a Mimikatz SSP log was written.
rules.recommendation: Delete the file securely after collecting it and reset the exposed credentials.

rules.title: File dropped in a Startup folder: {TargetFilename}
rules.description: A program or script was placed in a Startup folder, so it runs at every logon.
rules.recommendation: Review the file; remove it if it is not expected.

rules.title: {Image} loaded an unsigned DLL from a user-writable folder
rules.description: A process loaded an unsigned DLL from a folder normal users can write to. DLL sideloading uses a trusted program to load a malicious DLL like this.
rules.recommendation: Check the DLL hash and whether the program is expected to load it.

rules.title: Windows process {Image} loaded unsigned {ImageLoaded}
rules.description: A Windows binary loaded an unsigned DLL from System32. Everything Microsoft ships there is signed, so this is typically a planted DLL (search-order hijack).
rules.recommendation: Collect the DLL and find out how it was written to System32.

rules.title: {ParentImage} started {Image}
rules.description: An Office or PDF application launched a shell, script host or system utility. Malicious documents do this to run their payload.
rules.recommendation: Find the document that was open and quarantine it; check what the child process did.

rules.title: {ParentImage} started a shell (web shell or service exploitation)
rules.description: A server process (web server, SQL Server, print spooler, WinRM host) started a shell. This is how web shells, xp_cmdshell, spooler exploits and remote commands look on the target.
rules.recommendation: Review the command, the account it ran as and the server logs at that time.

rules.title: WMI started {Image} (remote WMI execution)
rules.description: WMI started a shell or script host. wmic /node, Impacket wmiexec and many worms run commands this way.
rules.recommendation: Correlate with network logons (4624 type 3) at the same time to find the source.

rules.title: UAC bypass: auto-elevating {ParentImage} started {Image}
rules.description: A Windows program that elevates without a UAC prompt started a shell or a program from a user folder. Fodhelper, eventvwr, sdclt and the other UACME techniques work this way.
rules.recommendation: Look for the hijacked registry key (HKCU\Software\Classes\...\shell\open\command) or planted DLL and remove it.

rules.title: {Image} has the name of a Windows binary but runs from the wrong folder
rules.description: A process named like a core Windows program ran from somewhere other than the Windows folder (or from a fake folder such as "C:\Windows \System32").
rules.recommendation: Collect the file and check its signature and hash.

rules.title: Renamed system tool: {Image} is really {OriginalFileName}
rules.description: The programs internal name does not match its file name. Attackers rename tools to dodge name-based detections.
rules.recommendation: Collect the file; review what it ran.

rules.title: UAC-bypass registry hijack: {TargetObject}
rules.description: A per-user registry key that auto-elevating Windows programs read was pointed at another command. Fodhelper, eventvwr, sdclt, WSReset and environment-variable UAC bypasses all start this way.
rules.recommendation: Delete the value, then find what it launched (look for an elevated shell right after).

rules.title: Security setting weakened: {TargetObject}
rules.description: A registry value that controls UAC, credential protection, Defender, RDP, Office macro access or PowerShell logging was changed.
rules.recommendation: Check the value against your baseline and revert it if the change was not planned.

rules.title: Security setting weakened: {TargetObject}
rules.description: A registry value that controls UAC, credential protection, Defender, RDP, Office macro access or PowerShell logging was changed.
rules.recommendation: Check the value against your baseline and revert it if the change was not planned.

rules.title: Persistence registry key set: {TargetObject}

match.TargetObject: (?i)\\Winlogon\\(?:Shell|Userinit|Notify)|\\Image File Execution Options\\[^\\]+\\(?:Debugger|GlobalFlag)$|\\SilentProcessExit\\[^\\]+\\MonitorProcess$|\\Windows\\AppInit_DLLs$|\\Control\\Lsa\\(?:Security Packages|Authentication Packages|Notification Packages)$|\\Control\\Print\\Monitors\\|\\Microsoft\\NetSh\\|\\Active Setup\\Installed Components\\[^\\]+\\StubPath$|\\User Shell Folders\\Startup$|\\Office test\\Special\\Perf|\\AppCompatFlags\\(?:Custom|InstalledSDB)\\|\\InprocServer32\\\(Default\)$|\\LocalServer32\\\(Default\)$|\\Services\\NTDS\\DirectoryServiceExtPt|\\LanmanServer\\Parameters\\NullSessionPipes$|\\Orchestrator\\UScheduler

rules.description: A value used by a known persistence or hijack technique was written: Winlogon, IFEO debugger, LSA packages, print monitors, netsh helpers, Active Setup, shims, COM servers, NTDS extensions or null-session pipes.
rules.recommendation: Review the value data and the writing process; remove it if unexpected.

rules.title: Account database or LSA secret modified: {TargetObject}
rules.description: The SAM or LSA secrets were changed directly in the registry (hidden $ account, RID hijack, machine-account secret). When the writer is not lsass.exe this is almost always malicious.
rules.recommendation: Check the account it belongs to and the process that wrote it.

rules.title: Port forwarding rule added: {TargetObject}
rules.description: A netsh portproxy rule forwards traffic through this host. Attackers use it to reach RDP or internal services from outside.
rules.recommendation: Remove the rule (netsh interface portproxy delete) and find who added it.

rules.title: Activity history key deleted: {TargetObject}
rules.description: A registry key that records user activity (Run dialog, recent documents, RDP history) was deleted. This is anti-forensics.
rules.recommendation: Use other sources (Prefetch, jump lists, shellbags) to rebuild the activity.

rules.title: Named pipe used for privilege escalation: {PipeName}
rules.description: A pipe name used by potato-style privilege escalation (PrintSpoofer, EfsPotato, RoguePotato), Kekeo, or PsExec-style remote execution was created or opened.
rules.recommendation: Identify the process that created the pipe and the account it ran as.

rules.title: BITS job downloading from {url}
rules.description: A BITS transfer fetched a program or archive from a raw IP or a file-sharing site. BITS downloads blend in with Windows Update traffic.
rules.recommendation: Find what started the job (bitsadmin, PowerShell, desktopimgdownldr) and the saved file.

rules.title: Compatibility shim applied to {ExePath}
rules.description: A compatibility fix was applied to an accessibility program that runs at the logon screen. Shim-based backdoors use this to get a SYSTEM shell before logon.
rules.recommendation: List installed shim databases (sdbinst / AppPatch\Custom) and remove unknown ones.

rules.title: Winsock provider (LSP) installed: {LSPName}
rules.description: A layered service provider was added to the Winsock catalog. It runs inside every program that uses the network.
rules.recommendation: Check the provider with netsh winsock show catalog; remove unknown ones.

rules.title: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) probe: MS_T120 channel requested
rules.description: An RDP client asked for the internal MS_T120 channel. Only BlueKeep scanners and exploits do this.
rules.recommendation: Patch CVE-2019-0708, block RDP from untrusted networks and find the scanning host.

rules.title: {param1} service stopped

match.param1|Param1: (?i)^(?:Windows Event Log|Sysmon64?|Microsoft Defender Antivirus Service|Windows Defender Antivirus Service|Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection Service)$

rules.description: The event log, Sysmon or Defender service stopped. Attackers stop or crash these to work without being recorded.
rules.recommendation: Check for a matching shutdown; otherwise find what stopped the service and look for a gap in the logs.

rules.title: SQL Server login failed for {Param1}
rules.description: A SQL Server login failed. Many of these from one client are a password-guessing attack on the database.
rules.recommendation: Check the client address and whether a successful login (18454/18453) followed.

rules.title: PowerShell restriction removed: {TargetObject}
rules.description: Constrained Language Mode was removed or the machine-wide execution policy was set to Unrestricted or Bypass.
rules.recommendation: Restore the policy and find the process that changed it.
